profiles.meeting_scenario: A preoperative planning meeting at a tertiary children's hospital for a 16-year-old girl with right-sided Poland's syndrome, including absent sternal head of the pectoralis major, marked infraclavicular hollowing, poor anterior axillary fold definition, breast hypoplasia, and suspected absence of the right 4th and 5th costochondral segments with mild ipsilateral sternal depression. The meeting is between the plastic/reconstructive service and the thoracic/chest wall service to coordinate a combined operation scheduled for mid-July. The agenda is to confirm what the first operation will include, what preoperative workup is assumed to be sufficient, how the chest wall base will be reconstructed before soft-tissue work, who handles which intraoperative steps, and the anticipated recovery pathway. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the first-stage surgery, assignment of responsibilities, and a timeline for imaging, booking, and postoperative follow-up.

members.name: Dr. Elena Markovic
members.expertise: Adolescent breast asymmetry, chest wall contour restoration, pedicled latissimus dorsi flaps, staged soft-tissue reconstruction
members.background: Leads the hospital's congenital chest and breast reconstruction clinic and routinely manages Poland's syndrome patients after puberty, often emphasizing visible contour symmetry and minimizing the number of aesthetic revisions.
members.private_state: She wants the first operation to accomplish as much visible improvement as possible before the patient starts her final year of school, and she is trying to avoid a plan that delays axillary fold correction into a separate surgery because families often perceive the chest wall repair alone as an incomplete result.
hidden_assumptions: The March low-dose chest CT already in the chart is the planning scan unless there are new respiratory symptoms.
A "solid base" is achieved when the reconstructed chest wall gives stable contour support for flap or expander placement without visible step-off or hardware show-through.
In a combined Poland reconstruction, recreating the anterior axillary fold belongs in the same first-stage operation if donor tissue is already being mobilized.
Once the chest wall scaffold is placed, the plastic surgery team effectively determines final soft-tissue extent, drain exit sites, and contour priorities.

members.name: Dr. Samuel Reed
members.expertise: Congenital chest wall deformities, rib and costochondral reconstruction, sternal stabilization, perioperative respiratory management
members.background: Directs the chest wall program and is accustomed to planning Poland-related operations around structural stability, pleural safety, and staged healing before cosmetic refinement.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid committing to aesthetic soft-tissue work before he confirms the exact extent of the costochondral defect and is concerned that adding contour work to the same stage could complicate respiratory monitoring and make any revision of the scaffold harder.
hidden_assumptions: Preoperative planning for adolescent costochondral agenesis requires a current dynamic chest CT close to the operation date, not just an older inspiratory scan.
A "solid base" means mechanically stable chest wall reconstruction with no clinically meaningful paradoxical motion during deep breathing or cough.
The first stage of a combined case should stop after skeletal reconstruction and durable coverage, with axillary fold and breast shaping treated as later aesthetic stages.
If the pleural space is entered or chest wall rigidity is altered, postoperative care should follow the thoracic pathway with chest drainage and higher-acuity overnight monitoring.

misalignment_points.topic: What "the CT" refers to for operative planning
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both casually refer to "the CT" as the imaging basis for planning.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the existing March low-dose inspiratory chest CT with 3D reconstruction already in the chart, which she considers adequate for symmetry planning and mirror-image contour work.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a fresh preoperative dynamic chest CT, ideally including inspiratory and expiratory assessment near the surgery date, because he expects to confirm the current extent of costochondral absence and sternal mechanics before finalizing the scaffold.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each specialty has a standard default when saying "the CT," and because both agree imaging exists and has been reviewed, neither feels a need to specify date, protocol, or purpose.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the first operation should create a "solid base" for soft-tissue reconstruction.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a chest wall platform that is smooth, visually stable, and firm enough to support the planned soft-tissue contour without tethering or visible depression under the flap or expander.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a biomechanically stable repair that abolishes clinically significant inward excursion or instability of the deficient costochondral area during respiration and coughing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from standard reconstructive language and sounds fully shared, but each surgeon silently applies a different specialty-specific threshold for adequacy without expecting to define it in a planning meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the "first stage" of the combined reconstruction
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about what they will do in the "first stage" or the "combined case" in July.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the July operation will include chest wall scaffold placement plus immediate creation of the anterior axillary fold with a pedicled latissimus transfer, while leaving final breast volume balancing for a later stage.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the July operation is limited to skeletal reconstruction and whatever soft-tissue coverage is necessary to protect the repair, with deliberate deferral of axillary fold recreation and other aesthetic contouring until healing is complete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both surgeons are comfortable with staged reconstruction and both expect more than one operation overall, saying "first stage" creates an illusion of agreement even though they draw the stage boundary differently.

turns.inner_thought: She is 16 and about to start her final school year, so the first operation needs to do more than just patch the chest wall. If we can place the scaffold and then use the latissimus in the same setting, I can correct the infraclavicular hollow and recreate the anterior axillary fold so the family sees a real visible change right away. For me, a solid base means a smooth, stable contour support without step-off or hardware show-through, something I can build on aesthetically from the start.
turns.utterance: From the reconstructive side, the big issues are the right-sided hollowing, the absent fold laterally, and the breast asymmetry. Since she's hoping to go into her last school year with things visibly improved, I'd like the July combined case to establish a solid base and move the contour forward in that first stage.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with July, but before I finalize anything I need a current dynamic chest CT close to the operation, not just an older inspiratory study. The key problem for me is the likely absence of the right 4th and 5th costochondral segments and how much instability or sternal mechanics are involved. When I say I've reviewed the CT, I mean the imaging set I expect to use for final structural planning once it is in the workflow.
turns.utterance: That timing makes sense to me. I've reviewed the CT, and the piece I'm most focused on is the missing mid-anterior support on the right and the mild sternal depression there, because that's going to drive how we set up the repair.

turns.inner_thought: The March low-dose CT with 3D recon already gives me what I need for mirror-image contour planning. I don't see a reason to repeat imaging unless her symptoms have changed. What I need from his reconstruction is a visually stable platform under the infraclavicular hollow and lateral chest so the flap sits cleanly and doesn't telegraph irregularities.
turns.utterance: The CT looked sufficient to me for planning the mirror-image contour. What I'd really need from the chest wall work is a solid base under that infraclavicular deficiency and out along the lateral chest so I can shape against it reliably.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on the goal, though to me a solid base means the repair is mechanically stable with no meaningful paradoxical motion once she is taking deep breaths and coughing after surgery. If the chest wall still moves abnormally, it does not matter how good it looks on the table.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely—that's exactly the goal. If we're doing this well, the first operation should leave her with a solid base, and I want that area behaving appropriately once she's breathing deeply and coughing afterward.

turns.inner_thought: Since the donor tissue will already be mobilized, it makes no sense to leave the anterior axillary fold for later; families read that as an incomplete reconstruction. In my mind, the first stage in July is chest wall scaffold plus immediate pedicled latissimus transfer to recreate the fold and improve the lateral contour, with breast volume balancing deferred.
turns.utterance: In terms of sequencing, in the first stage I would plan to use the latissimus while we're already there so we can bring back the anterior axillary fold, and then leave the final breast volume work for later.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds fine at a high level because I still understand the first stage as stopping after skeletal reconstruction and whatever coverage is needed to protect it. I do not want to commit to broader contour work before I know exactly what the defect requires, and if the pleural space is entered I need a straightforward recovery course. Durable coverage is one thing; aesthetic refinement is later.
turns.utterance: That sequencing sounds reasonable. For me, in the first stage the priority is to complete the structural repair and make sure it has durable coverage before we worry about the rest of the contour.

turns.inner_thought: Once his scaffold is in, I expect the plastic team to take over the extent of the soft-tissue work, contour priorities, and drain placement on our side. If I can mark the fold position and infraclavicular fill intraoperatively, I can make the result look substantially improved at the end of that first operation.
turns.utterance: That works. Once the framework is in place, I can take the lead on the soft-tissue shaping and mark where I want the fold and the upper-chest fill to sit so the reconstruction reads properly.

turns.inner_thought: Before booking is finalized, I need the CT loaded into my planning workflow so I can size the defect repair from a current study and decide whether this needs chest drainage and higher-acuity overnight monitoring under the thoracic pathway. I'm assuming that step is obvious when I say I need the CT for planning.
turns.utterance: Good. Before we lock the booking, I do want the CT loaded into my planning workflow so I can size the repair properly and get a handle on what her postoperative monitoring is likely to need.

turns.inner_thought: I'll speak to the family as if the July plan is based on the March CT already in the chart. I want them prepared for staged reconstruction overall, but I also want them expecting that the first stage will create the visible foundation—chest wall support plus fold restoration—not just an internal repair they can't appreciate.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll consent the family for staged reconstruction in July based on the CT we already have, and I'll explain that the first stage is about establishing the foundation for the final result.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. My team will do the chest wall portion first, aiming for a mechanically stable repair that gives her a dependable base. After that, whatever soft-tissue work is appropriate can proceed, but I still think of the July stage primarily as the structural operation with thoracic postoperative oversight if indicated.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We'll be ready in July to do the chest wall portion first so we can give you the base you need, and then we can hand over for the rest of the case.
